title: Fermat and Euler from Lagrange
objectives: Prove Fermat’s little theorem and Euler’s theorem from Lagrange’s theorem.

screens.title: Powers that cycle
screens.prose: We want $2^{100} \bmod 7$ by hand. Start with small powers. The grid holds $a^k \bmod 7$ for bases 1 to 6, except row 2. In row 2, each power is the one before times 2, reduced mod 7.
screens.question: Fill in $2^k \bmod 7$ for $k = 1$ to $6$.

hints.text: Double the previous value and take away 7 if needed.

feedback.correct: Right. The powers of 2 cycle 2, 4, 1 with period 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reduce each power modulo 7.

byKey.raw4: You wrote $2^k$ before reducing. Take away multiples of 7 to land in 0 to 6.
byKey.raw5: You wrote $2^k$ before reducing. Take away multiples of 7 to land in 0 to 6.
byKey.raw6: You wrote $2^k$ before reducing. Take away multiples of 7 to land in 0 to 6.

explain.text: $2^3 = 8 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$, so the powers repeat every 3 steps. Row 2 reads 2, 4, 1, 2, 4, 1. The period is 3.

screens.title: A large power
screens.prose: The powers of 2 repeat with period 3, and $100 = 33 \times 3 + 1$. So $2^{100} = (2^3)^{33} \cdot 2$.
screens.question: What is $2^{100} \bmod 7$?

hints.text: What is left is the single factor 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 100 by the period 3 and keep the remainder.

byKey.mod7: You reduced the exponent modulo 7, giving $2^2$. Exponents repeat with the period of the powers, here 3, not with the modulus.
byKey.one: You assumed the cycle ends exactly at 100. $100 = 33 \times 3 + 1$, so one factor of 2 is left.

explain.text: $2^{100} = (2^3)^{33} \cdot 2 \equiv 1^{33} \cdot 2 = 2 \pmod 7$. Only the exponent modulo the period matters. Every period in the grid divides 6.

screens.title: Every period divides 6
screens.prose: Each row of the grid cycles. Its period is the order $\operatorname{ord}(a)$ of $a$ in $\mathbb{Z}_7^{\times}$, the first $k$ with $a^k \equiv 1$.
screens.question: Tap the first 1 in each row.

hints.text: Read each row from the left until you meet 1.
The first 1s sit in columns 1, 3, 6, 3, 6 and 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap one cell per row: the first that reads 1.

explain.text: The orders are 1, 3, 6, 3, 6 and 2. Each one divides 6, the number of units mod 7. So column 6 is all 1s.

screens.title: Fermat's little theorem
screens.prose: Every order divided $6 = 7 - 1$, so $a^6 \equiv 1$ for every row. In general, **Fermat's little theorem**: $$a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p \quad \text{for a prime } p \text{ and } p \nmid a.$$
screens.question: Why must every order divide 6?

options.text: $\operatorname{ord}(a) = |\langle a \rangle|$, and Lagrange says it divides $|\mathbb{Z}_7^{\times}| = 6$.

options.why: You looked at parity. Order 3 is odd and still divides 6; evenness plays no part.
Primality makes all six non-zero residues units. The dividing itself comes from Lagrange.

options.text: Because powers of a residue always cycle.
options.why: Cycling gives a period. It does not say why the period divides 6.

hints.text: Lagrange (l7): a subgroup's size divides the group's size.

feedback.correct: Right. Fermat is Lagrange applied to the units.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of $\langle a \rangle$ as a subgroup.

explain.text: $\langle a \rangle$ is a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_7^{\times}$ with $\operatorname{ord}(a)$ elements. Lagrange makes $\operatorname{ord}(a)$ divide 6. So $a^6 = 1$ in every row.

screens.title: Proving Fermat
screens.prose: Now for any prime $p$. Recall from l3 that every non-zero residue modulo a prime has an inverse. One line below is flawed.
screens.question: Prove $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ for $p \nmid a$. Leave out the flawed line.

lines.text: Let $p$ be prime and $p \nmid a$, so $a \in \mathbb{Z}_p^{\times}$ (setup).
$\mathbb{Z}_p^{\times}$ is a group with $p - 1$ elements (l3: every non-zero residue is a unit).
Write $p - 1 = k \operatorname{ord}(a)$ for a whole number $k$ (definition of divides).

lines.why: The group under multiplication is the units, with $p - 1$ elements. 0 has no inverse.

hints.text: Lagrange gives $\operatorname{ord}(a) \mid p - 1$; then raise $a^{\operatorname{ord}(a)} = 1$ to the power $k$.

feedback.correct: Right. Fermat follows from Lagrange in four steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name the group $\mathbb{Z}_p^{\times}$, apply Lagrange, then use the order.

byKey.d1: You used $\mathbb{Z}_p$ with $p$ elements. Under multiplication the group is $\mathbb{Z}_p^{\times}$, without 0, with $p - 1$ elements.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: The units mod $p$ form a group of size $p - 1$. Lagrange makes $\operatorname{ord}(a)$ divide $p - 1$. Raising $a^{\operatorname{ord}(a)} = 1$ to the $k$th power gives $a^{p-1} = 1$.

screens.title: Euler's theorem
screens.prose: Euler's $\varphi(n) = |\mathbb{Z}_n^{\times}|$ counts the residues coprime to $n$. **Euler's theorem**: if $\gcd(a, n) = 1$ then $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n$. The proof is Fermat's with a new group. The first two lines may come in either order.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: $\mathbb{Z}_n^{\times}$ is a group with $\varphi(n)$ elements (definition of $\varphi$).

lines.why: Lagrange uses the size of the group of units, $\varphi(n)$. That equals $n - 1$ only when $n$ is prime.

feedback.correct: Right. Fermat is the case $n = p$, where $\varphi(p) = p - 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow Fermat's proof with $\mathbb{Z}_n^{\times}$ in place of $\mathbb{Z}_p^{\times}$.

byKey.d1: You used $n - 1$. The group of units has $\varphi(n)$ elements, which is smaller when $n$ is composite.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: Only the group changes: $\mathbb{Z}_n^{\times}$ has $\varphi(n)$ elements. Lagrange gives $\operatorname{ord}(a) \mid \varphi(n)$, so $a^{\varphi(n)} = 1$. For prime $n = p$, $\varphi(p) = p - 1$ and this is Fermat.

screens.title: Counting units
screens.prose: $\varphi(n)$ counts the $a$ from 1 to $n - 1$ with $\gcd(a, n) = 1$. The table gives the gcds. Then Euler predicts a power.
screens.question: Find $\varphi(9)$, $\varphi(12)$ and $5^4 \bmod 12$.

hints.text: Count the 1s in each row of the gcd table.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count only the residues coprime to $n$.

byKey.nminus1: You counted every residue from 1 to 8. The multiples of 3 share a factor with 9.
byKey.nminus1b: You counted 1 to 11. Only 1, 5, 7 and 11 are coprime to 12.

explain.text: The units mod 9 are 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, so $\varphi(9) = 6$. The units mod 12 are 1, 5, 7, 11, so $\varphi(12) = 4$. Euler then gives $5^4 = 625 \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$.

screens.title: A last digit
screens.prose: The last digit of a number is its residue mod 10. Here $\gcd(7, 10) = 1$ and $\varphi(10) = 4$, since the units are 1, 3, 7, 9. This is an interview staple.
screens.question: What is the last digit of $7^{222}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reduce the exponent modulo 4, then read the table.

byKey.three: You took the remainder of 222 by 4 as 3. $222 = 55 \times 4 + 2$, so the remainder is 2.
byKey.one: You assumed 4 divides 222. It leaves remainder 2.

explain.text: $7^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{10}$ by Euler, and $222 = 55 \times 4 + 2$. So $7^{222} \equiv 7^2 = 49 \equiv 9$. The last digit is 9.

screens.title: The wrong exponent
screens.prose: A tempting shortcut is $a^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ for any $n$. Test it with $a = 2$ and $n = 9$. The table shows the powers of 2 mod 9 up to $k = 6$.
screens.question: What is $2^8 \bmod 9$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $2^6 \equiv 1$ and multiply by $2^2$.

byKey.shortcut: You used $a^{n-1} \equiv 1$. That is Fermat's form, which needs $n$ prime; for $n = 9$ the exponent is $\varphi(9) = 6$.

explain.text: $2^8 = 256 = 28 \times 9 + 4$, so $2^8 \equiv 4$. Euler's exponent is $\varphi(9) = 6$, and indeed $2^6 \equiv 1$. The exponent $n - 1$ works for prime $n$ only.

screens.title: RSA in miniature
screens.prose: RSA signs and encrypts messages, for example to authenticate an order sent to a broker. Take $n = 33 = 3 \times 11$, so $\varphi(33) = 2 \times 10 = 20$. The public exponent is 3 and the private one is 7, since $3 \times 7 = 21 \equiv 1 \pmod{20}$. A message $m$ is sent as $m^3 \bmod 33$.
screens.question: Encrypt the message 4, then decrypt the result.

feedback.correct: Right. 4 goes to 31 and comes back to 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reduce each power modulo 33.

byKey.cube: You raised 31 to the public exponent 3, which gives 25. Decryption uses the private exponent 7.
byKey.copy: You copied the ciphertext. Raise 31 to the private exponent 7 and reduce mod 33.

explain.text: $4^3 = 64 \equiv 31$, and $31^7 \equiv (-2)^7 = -128 \equiv 4 \pmod{33}$. Decryption works because $4^{21} = 4 \cdot (4^{20}) \equiv 4$ by Euler. Real keys use primes with hundreds of digits.

screens.title: Fermat liars
screens.prose: A base $a$ with $\gcd(a, n) = 1$ and $a^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ is a Fermat liar for composite $n$. A **Carmichael number** is a composite $n$ for which every coprime base lies. Checking every base proves the claim for that one $n$ only.
screens.question: Complete `fermat_liars(n)` and `is_carmichael(n)`.

tests.call: next(n for n in range(3, 2001) if is_carmichael(n))

widget.how: The first Check starts Python, which takes a few seconds. Submit runs 10 hidden tests; each must equal the expected value exactly.

hints.text: Keep $a$ when `gcd(a, n) == 1` and `pow(a, n - 1, n) == 1`.
A Carmichael number is composite and has as many liars as units.
For 561, every one of the $\varphi(561) = 320$ units is a liar.

feedback.correct: Right. 561 fools every coprime base; 341 is caught by base 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Filter by gcd and by the Fermat test, and exclude primes from Carmichael.

explain.text: For 15 only 1, 4, 11 and 14 lie. 341 passes base 2 but $3^{340} \equiv 56$, so it is not Carmichael. 561 is the smallest Carmichael number.

ideas: The order of $a$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n^{\times}$ divides $|\mathbb{Z}_n^{\times}| = \varphi(n)$ by Lagrange, so $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1$ when $\gcd(a, n) = 1$.
For a prime $p$ and $p \nmid a$ this is Fermat: $a^{p-1} \equiv 1$. Then $a^p \equiv a$ for every $a$, and $a^{-1} \equiv a^{p-2}$.
Reduce exponents modulo $\varphi(n)$, or modulo the order: $7^{222} \equiv 7^2 \equiv 9 \pmod{10}$.

formula.name: Euler's theorem
formula.note: Fermat is the case $n = p$, $\varphi(p) = p - 1$.

summary.trap: Using $a^{n-1} \equiv 1$ for composite $n$: $2^8 \equiv 4 \pmod 9$. The right exponent is $\varphi(9) = 6$.

quiz.prose: By Fermat, $3^6 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$, so $3 \cdot 3^5 \equiv 1$ and $3^{-1} \equiv 3^5$. This is the inverse $a^{p-2}$ from `contests` l5.
quiz.question: What is $3^{-1} \bmod 7$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $3^5 = 243$ and reduce it mod 7.

byKey.raw: You stopped at 243. Reduce it modulo 7.

explain.text: $3^5 = 243 = 34 \times 7 + 5$, so $3^{-1} \equiv 5$. Check: $3 \times 5 = 15 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$. Fermat gives the inverse as $a^{p-2}$.

options.text: The converse of Fermat fails: a composite can pass for one base, and base 3 exposes it.

options.why: You trusted one base. $341 = 11 \times 31$, and base 3 gives 56, not 1.
You reversed the theorem. Fermat speaks about primes; 341 is composite, so nothing is contradicted.

options.text: Every coprime base will pass for 341.
options.why: That describes a Carmichael number such as $561 = 3 \times 11 \times 17$. For 341, base 3 fails.

feedback.correct: Right. Passing a Fermat test is evidence, not proof.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fermat says primes pass; it does not say only primes pass.

explain.text: Fermat says every prime passes, not that only primes pass. 341 passes base 2 and fails base 3. 561 passes every coprime base; a shared factor such as 3 gives $3^{560} \equiv 375$.

quiz.prose: In the RSA example, $n = 33$, $\varphi(33) = 20$, and the exponents are 3 and 7. Take $m$ with $\gcd(m, 33) = 1$.
quiz.question: Order the reasons that $(m^3)^7 \equiv m \pmod{33}$.

feedback.correct: Right. Euler undoes the extra 20 in the exponent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $21 = 1 + 20$, split the power, then apply Euler.

explain.text: $21 = 1 + 20$ splits $m^{21}$ into $m \cdot m^{20}$. Euler makes $m^{20} \equiv 1$. So decryption returns $m$.

quiz.prose: From Fermat, $a^p \equiv a \pmod p$ for $p \nmid a$: multiply $a^{p-1} \equiv 1$ by $a$.
quiz.question: Does $a^7 \equiv a \pmod 7$ also hold for $a = 14$?

options.text: Yes. Both sides are 0 mod 7, so it holds for every $a$.

options.why: You applied the hypothesis of $a^{p-1} \equiv 1$. The form $a^p \equiv a$ also holds when $p \mid a$, as $0 \equiv 0$.
You used $a^{p-1} \equiv 1$ for a multiple of 7. Here $14 \equiv 0$, so $14^7 \equiv 0$.
Parity plays no part. Multiples of 7 give 0 on both sides.

feedback.correct: Right. $a^p \equiv a$ holds for every integer $a$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reduce 14 mod 7 first.

explain.text: $14 \equiv 0 \pmod 7$, so both $14^7$ and $14$ are $0 \bmod 7$. So $a^p \equiv a$ holds for every $a$. Only $a^{p-1} \equiv 1$ needs $p \nmid a$.
